summary: Describes the method for encoding Korean characters in both the headers and bodies of Internet mail messages. The method had been in use since 1991 and had become widely used in Korean IP networks.

plainLanguage.summary: This memo documents a method for encoding Korean in Internet mail. It uses control codes to switch between ASCII and KSC 5601 in message bodies, and specifies a different encoding for headers.

questions: how to send korean text in mail
how does korean email switch between ascii and hangul
subtitle: The ISO-2022-KR encoding method for Korean text in Internet messages.

tldr.problem: Internet mail needed a documented method for representing Korean characters in message bodies and headers.
tldr.mechanism: The body encoding switches between ASCII and KSC 5601 using ESC, SO, and SI controls. The memo names the body charset ISO-2022-KR and describes a separate EUC-KR method for headers.
tldr.outcome: RFC 1557 records an encoding method that had been in use since 1991 and was used in Korean IP networks. It is informational.

today: The unit metadata lists RFC 1557 as Informational and records no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The memo describes a Korean mail encoding method.

sections.title: The Korean Mail Encoding
sections.content:
The RFC describes an encoding method used for Korean characters in the headers and bodies of Internet mail. The method was specified in 1991 and, according to the memo, had since been widely used in Korean IP networks.

The document covers plain text only. Rich text and other text subtypes are outside its scope.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo writes down a Korean mail encoding already in use. It covers plain text messages, not rich text formats.

sections.title: Switching Between ASCII and Korean
sections.content:
The message begins in ASCII. The escape sequence ESC $ ) C appears once at the beginning of a line before any SO character. SO marks following characters as Korean in KSC 5601; SI returns to ASCII. Each KSC 5601 character is two bytes long.

The encoding name for message-body content is ISO-2022-KR. The RFC says the encoding is 7-bit in nature, so a content-transfer-encoding header is not required for the body.
sections.plainLanguage: Control codes mark when the body switches from ASCII to Korean and back. The body charset name is ISO-2022-KR.

sections.title: MIME Bodies and Message Headers
sections.content:
For a MIME body, the memo gives the form Content-Type: text/plain; charset=iso-2022-kr. It notes that then-current Korean message software did not support Base64 or quoted-printable applied to already encoded Hangul messages.

For Korean in message headers, the RFC specifies EUC-KR. The encoded header text is then B- or Q-encoded using the method proposed in RFC 1522, with the name EUC-KR.
sections.plainLanguage: The body uses ISO-2022-KR. Header text uses EUC-KR and is then encoded with the MIME header method described in RFC 1522.
